name: Giuoco Pianissimo
summary: The Giuoco Pianissimo (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.Nc3) is the restrained modern Italian, building slowly with d3.
intro: The Giuoco Pianissimo, literally the 'very quiet game', arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.d3 Nf6 5.Nc3. Rather than the sharp c3-and-d4 break of the older Giuoco Piano, White plays the modest d3 and aims for a slow manoeuvring build-up. This restrained approach has become the mainstream way of handling the Italian at every level of modern play.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5 d3 Nf6 Nc3

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The defining choice is 4.d3, a quiet move that supports the e4-pawn and the c4-bishop while declining the immediate central confrontation. Instead of striking with c3 and d4 at once, White prepares a long, patient build-up, keeping the pawn structure flexible and the tension low. The point is to reach a rich middlegame where understanding and manoeuvring matter more than memorised theory, and where White retains the option to expand in the centre or on the kingside only when fully prepared. Both sides usually complete development harmoniously before any pawns are committed.

A hallmark plan for White is the manoeuvre c3 followed by Nbd2-f1-g3, rerouting the queen's knight toward the kingside exactly as in the Ruy López, often combined with a later d4 break or a slow kingside pawn advance. White typically tucks the king away with O-O and Re1, sometimes retreating the c4-bishop to b3 to keep it safe from ...Na5. Black mirrors much of this with ...d6, ...a6, ...Ba7 or ...Bb6, and ...O-O, aiming for a solid, elastic set-up. The game becomes a battle of small improvements, with the eventual central break by either side defining the middlegame.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The named position with 5.Nc3 is the Italian Four Knights, a symmetrical, solid structure in which both sides have developed knights to their natural squares and the play remains balanced and manoeuvring. More topical at master level is the flexible move order with 4.d3 followed by c3 and Nbd2 rather than an early Nc3, keeping the c-pawn free to support a d4 advance and the knight ready to reroute via f1 to g3 or e3. Black's most reliable replies involve ...d6, ...a6, and ...Ba7, retreating the bishop to safety and preparing ...O-O with a resilient position.

From these set-ups a range of standard middlegame plans emerges. White may prepare the d4 break to open the centre, expand on the kingside, or manoeuvre for pressure against the e5-pawn and the sensitive f7-square; Black counters with ...d5 breaks of his own, queenside expansion via ...a5 and ...b5, or piece play against White's centre. Because nothing is forced in the early moves, transpositions abound and the Pianissimo frequently blends into related Italian and even Ruy López structures. This transpositional flexibility is a large part of its modern appeal.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Italian Game is among the oldest recorded openings, and the Giuoco Piano was extensively analysed by masters such as Greco in the seventeenth century, but the ultra-quiet Pianissimo treatment came into its own much later. After the sharp c3-d4 lines were largely neutralised by theory, elite players rediscovered the slow d3 systems as a way to reach fresh, strategically complex middlegames without conceding early equality. In the modern era it has become one of the most popular replies to 1.e4 e5, championed by many top grandmasters precisely because it steers the game toward understanding rather than forcing lines.

keyIdeas: 4.d3 declines the sharp d4 break in favour of a slow, restrained build-up.
White reroutes the queen's knight via d2-f1-g3, as in the Ruy López.
The pawn structure stays flexible, with a d4 break saved for later.
Both sides develop harmoniously before committing to a central plan.
Retreating the bishop to b3 (or ...Ba7) keeps it safe and preserves tension.
Rich in transpositions to other Italian and Spanish structures.

white: Complete development with O-O and Re1 before committing pawns.
Manoeuvre the b1-knight via d2-f1-g3 toward the kingside.
Prepare c3 and a well-timed d4 to expand in the centre.
Tuck the light-squared bishop back to b3 to dodge ...Na5.
Play patiently for small improvements and pressure on e5 and f7.
black: Castle short and prepare the freeing ...d5 break.
Expand on the queenside with ...a5 and ...b5 when appropriate.
Mirror White's knight manoeuvres and contest the centre.
Keep the position elastic and avoid premature commitments.
